model: claude-opus-5-5 (Claude Code general-purpose subagent, instructions in the task prompt)
opening: Drill me on git rebase vs merge until I actually get it.

turns.text:
Deal. Here's the ground we'll cover:

1. Commit graph basics: commits, parents, branches as pointers, HEAD
2. What `git merge` actually does: fast-forward vs. three-way merge, merge commits
3. What `git rebase` actually does: replaying commits, new hashes
4. Resulting history shape: linear vs. branching, what `git log` shows
5. Conflict handling in each: when conflicts show up and how often
6. The golden rule: rewriting shared history, force-push, and the danger it creates
7. Interactive rebase: squash, reorder, edit, fixup
8. Choosing between them: team workflows, pull `--rebase`, and the trade-offs

First I'll ask a few questions, one at a time, to see what you already know. I won't teach anything until that's done. Then I'll show you a skill map and suggest where to start.

Question 1:

You're on branch `feature`, which split off from `main` three commits ago. Since then, `main` has gotten two new commits. In your own words, what is a branch in git, physically? What actually gets stored when you create one?
I think a branch is basically just a pointer to a commit, like a label with the commit hash in it. When I make a new commit on it, the pointer just moves forward to the new one.

That's right. A branch is just a small ref holding one commit hash, and committing moves it forward. I'll come back later to check what "forward" means for the parent links.

Question 2:

Same setup. `feature` has 3 commits of its own, and `main` has 2 new commits since the split. You're on `feature` and run `git merge main`. Describe the commit graph afterward. Is there a new commit? If so, how many parents does it have, and which commits are they? Where do `feature` and `main` point now?

Yeah, I think there's a new merge commit on feature, and it has two parents: my last feature commit and the latest commit on main. Then feature moves to point at that merge commit, and main stays where it was.

Correct. The merge commit has two parents, your last `feature` commit and the tip of `main`. `feature` moves to it and `main` stays put.

Question 3:

Back to the starting point, before any merge. You're on `feature` (3 commits of its own, `main` has 2 new ones) and you run `git rebase main` instead. Describe the graph afterward. What happens to your 3 feature commits? Do they keep their original commit hashes? Where do `feature` and `main` point now?

My 3 feature commits get moved over on top of the latest main commit, so the history looks like a straight line. They keep the same hashes since it's the same commits, git just moves the feature pointer to sit after main's tip. Main stays where it was.

You got part of it right. The result is a straight line, `feature` ends up after `main`'s tip, and `main` doesn't move. But the claim that the commits keep their hashes is the part I want to test, so I'm not going to tell you yet whether it's right.

Question 3b:

A commit's hash is computed from the commit object's contents. List everything you think goes into a commit object. Then tell me: before the rebase, what was the parent of your first feature commit, and what is its parent after the rebase?
I'd guess the commit object has the snapshot of the files, the author, the timestamp, and the commit message. Since none of that changes when you rebase, the hash should stay the same, right?

Your reasoning holds up: if nothing in the commit object changes, the hash can't change. So the question is whether your list is complete. You answered the first half of my question but skipped the second half, and that's where the answer is.

Go back to Question 1. You said committing "moves the pointer forward to the new one." But a branch only stores one hash, the tip. So when you run `git log` and git walks backward from the tip through older and older commits, where does it find out which commit came before each one?

Answer that, then tell me: is that piece of information the same for your first feature commit before and after the rebase?

Hmm, I guess each commit must store the hash of its parent, otherwise git couldn't walk backward. And before the rebase my first feature commit's parent was the old commit on main where I branched, but after it's main's new tip... so that's different, which would mean the hash actually changes?

Yes, the hash changes. Each commit stores its parent's hash, so it's part of what gets hashed. Rebase gives your first feature commit a new parent, which makes it a new commit with a new hash. Commit 2's parent is now that new commit, so its hash changes too, and the same goes for commit 3. Rebase doesn't move your commits. It makes 3 new copies on top of `main`, moves `feature` to the last copy, and leaves the originals behind with no branch pointing at them.

For the record, you got there with a lot of nudging, so I'm counting this as "can follow along," not "knows it cold." We'll come back to it.

Question 4:

Say you had already pushed `feature` to the shared remote before rebasing, and a teammate pulled it and started building their own commits on top of your old commit 3. You rebase onto `main` and try `git push`. What happens to that push, and if you force it through, what problem does your teammate run into the next time they pull?

Hmm, I think the push would get rejected because the remote still has the old commit 3 and my branch doesn't have it anymore, so it's not a fast-forward. If I force it, I'm honestly not sure what goes wrong for my teammate, wouldn't their pull just grab the new copies and carry on?

The first half is right. The remote's `feature` still ends at old commit 3, your local `feature` doesn't contain it, so it isn't a fast-forward and the push gets rejected.

For the second half, use what you just worked out about hashes.

Question 4b:

After your force-push, your teammate's local branch has the old commits 1, 2, 3 (original hashes) with their own work on top. The remote now has `main`'s 2 new commits followed by your rebased copies 1', 2', 3' (new hashes). They run `git pull`, which by default fetches and then merges the remote branch into theirs.

When git compares the two histories, does it know that 1 and 1' are "the same change"? Based on that, what does their history look like after the pull, and what will they see when they run `git log`?

Since 1' has a different hash than 1, I guess git wouldn't know they're the same change, it'd just see them as different commits. So the merge would pull in 1', 2', 3' alongside their old 1, 2, 3, and git log would show my commits twice? That seems messy, but I'm not totally sure that's what actually happens.

That's what actually happens, and you worked it out from the hash rule instead of guessing. Git compares commits by hash. 1 and 1' have different hashes, so git sees them as unrelated commits. The pull makes a merge commit that joins both lines, and `git log` shows each of your changes twice, with the same message and author but different hashes. If your teammate then pushes, the duplicates end up on the shared branch for everyone. Because 1' sits on top of `main`'s new commits and 1 doesn't, that merge can also produce conflicts in code your teammate never touched.

This is why the rule is "don't rebase commits other people already have." We'll go deeper into it later.

Question 5 (last diagnostic question):

Back to the clean setup: `feature` has 3 commits, `main` has 2 new ones, and nothing has been pushed. All 3 of your feature commits edit the same line in `config.py`, and one of `main`'s new commits also changed that line.

If you run `git merge main`, how many times might you have to stop and resolve a conflict? If you run `git rebase main` instead, how many times might you have to stop? Explain why the two numbers differ (or don't).
